title: Fluid Mechanics / Hydrostatics

notes.heading: 1. Hydrostatic Pressure, Pascal's Law & Archimedes' Floatation
notes.proseLatex: Absolute pressure at depth $h$ in an incompressible static liquid of density $\rho$ is $P = P_0 + \rho g h$ (gauge pressure $= \rho g h$, depending ONLY on vertical depth, never container shape!). Pascal's law transmits enclosed pressure undiminished, giving hydraulic mechanical advantage $F_2/F_1 = A_2/A_1$. By Archimedes' principle, upward buoyant thrust equals the weight of displaced fluid $F_B = V_{\text{sub}}\rho_f g$; a solid floats in equilibrium with submerged fraction $\frac{V_{\text{sub}}}{V} = \frac{\rho_s}{\rho_f}$.

keyFormulas.label: Hydrostatic Pressure, Hydraulic Lift & Floating Fraction
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Compute gauge/absolute pressure, hydraulic force multiplication, and floating submergence.

examples.problemLatex: An iceberg ($\rho_i = 0.90\text{ g/cm}^3$) floats in sea water ($\rho_w = 1.025\text{ g/cm}^3$). What fraction of its volume stays ABOVE the water surface?

notes.heading: 2. Continuity Equation, Bernoulli's Theorem & Torricelli's Efflux
notes.proseLatex: For steady incompressible flow, volume conservation gives $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 = Q$ ($\text{m}^3/\text{s}$). Along a streamline of ideal non-viscous flow, Bernoulli's equation $P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{const}$ expresses mechanical energy conservation per unit volume. Applying Bernoulli to a small orifice at depth $h$ below an open wide tank gives Torricelli's efflux speed $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ (identical to free-fall speed from height $h$!).

keyFormulas.label: Continuity, Bernoulli's Equation & Torricelli Speed
keyFormulas.latex: $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2,\qquad P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{const},\qquad v_{\text{efflux}} = \sqrt{2gh}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Solve Venturi-meter pressure drops and tank-orifice jet speeds.

notes.heading: 3. Newton's Viscosity, Poiseuille's Law & Stokes' Terminal Velocity
notes.proseLatex: Viscous shear force between laminar layers is $F = -\eta A\frac{dv}{dy}$ where $\eta$ has SI unit $\text{Pa\,s}$ ($1\text{ Pa\,s} = 10\text{ poise}$). Laminar tube flow obeys Poiseuille's $R^4$ law $Q = \frac{\pi \Delta P\,R^4}{8\eta L}$, while Reynolds number $\text{Re} = \frac{\rho v D}{\eta}$ separates laminar from turbulent regimes. A sphere of radius $r$ and density $\rho$ falling through fluid of density $\sigma$ experiences Stokes' drag $F_d = 6\pi\eta r v$ and settles at terminal velocity $v_T \propto r^2$.

keyFormulas.label: Stokes' Drag & Terminal Velocity Scaling
keyFormulas.latex: $F_d = 6\pi\eta r v,\qquad v_T = \frac{2 r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta},\qquad Q_{\text{pipe}} = \frac{\pi \Delta P\,R^4}{8\eta L}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Scale terminal velocity when droplets coalesce (n^(2/3) scaling!) and pipe flow with R^4.

examples.problemLatex: Eight identical raindrops each having terminal speed $2\text{ cm/s}$ coalesce into one bigger drop. Find the new terminal speed.

wbjeebTraps: When pure ice floating in pure water melts completely, the water level remains UNCHANGED (displaced water volume already equals melted water volume!).
Unit conversion trap: $1\text{ poise} = 0.1\text{ Pa\,s}$ (NOT $10\text{ Pa\,s}$).
Temperature trend flip: heating DECREASES viscosity of liquids (cohesive bonds weaken) but INCREASES viscosity of gases ($\eta_{\text{gas}} \propto \sqrt{T}$).

conceptPrimer.heading: Hydrostatic Pressure: Depth, Not Shape
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Static liquid pressure at vertical depth $h$ is $P = P_0 + \rho g h$; the gauge part $\rho g h$ depends ONLY on $h$, $\rho$ and $g$ — never on the container shape or total volume (hydrostatic paradox: a skinny tube and a wide lake at the same depth carry the same pressure). Absolute pressure adds atmospheric $P_0 \approx 1.013 \times 10^5\ \text{Pa}$; most JELET answers want gauge pressure unless stated. Micro-check: $10\ \text{m}$ down in water with $\rho = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$: gauge pressure $= 1000 \times 10 \times 10 = 10^5\ \text{Pa} = 100\ \text{kPa}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Pascal's Law and the Hydraulic Press
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: An enclosed liquid at rest transmits an externally applied pressure change UNCHANGED to every point and wall — that is Pascal's law, and it powers hydraulic presses and brakes: $\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$, so a small force on a small piston becomes a large force on a large piston, paying for it with a proportionally larger displacement. Micro-check: $20\ \text{N}$ on a $5\ \text{cm}^2$ piston gives $4\ \text{N/cm}^2$; transmitted intact to a $50\ \text{cm}^2$ piston it lifts $4 \times 50 = 200\ \text{N}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Archimedes, Floatation and the Ice-Water Trick
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A immersed body feels upthrust equal to the WEIGHT of displaced fluid; floating requires weight = upthrust, so the submerged fraction is $\frac{V_{\text{sub}}}{V} = \frac{\rho_{\text{body}}}{\rho_{\text{fluid}}}$. The classic WBJEE trap: ice floating in water has already displaced exactly the water its melted form will occupy, so the LEVEL STAYS UNCHANGED when it melts — it rises only if the ice carries trapped heavier mass or sits in a liquid lighter than water. Micro-check: ice of density $0.9\rho_w$ floats with $\tfrac{0.9\rho_w}{\rho_w} = \tfrac{9}{10}$ of its volume submerged.

conceptPrimer.heading: Continuity: Area-Speed Conservation
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: For steady incompressible flow the volume rate is constant everywhere: $Q = A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$ ($\text{m}^3/\text{s}$). Since $A = \pi r^2$, halving the RADIUS quarters the area and QUADRUPLES the speed — a favourite numerical. Velocity is largest where the pipe is narrowest. Micro-check: $3\ \text{m/s}$ in a pipe of radius $2\ \text{cm}$ becomes $3 \times 4 = 12\ \text{m/s}$ where the radius is $1\ \text{cm}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Bernoulli's Theorem and Torricelli's Efflux
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Along a streamline of ideal (non-viscous, steady, incompressible) flow, $P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{const}$ — pressure head, speed head and height head trade against each other. On a horizontal streamline, faster flow means LOWER pressure (aerofoil lift, venturimeter). For a tank with an orifice at depth $h$ below the free surface, Bernoulli gives Torricelli's efflux speed $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ — the same speed as a free fall from that depth. Micro-check: a hole $5\ \text{m}$ deep jets out at $v = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 5} = 10\ \text{m/s}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Viscosity: Newton, Poiseuille and Stokes
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Viscous shear between laminar layers is $F = -\eta A\frac{dv}{dy}$ with SI unit $\text{Pa\,s}$ ($1\ \text{Pa\,s} = 10\ \text{poise}$ — the conversion trap runs the other way). Heating WEAKENS liquids (viscosity falls) but SCATTERS gases harder (viscosity rises). Laminar tube flow obeys Poiseuille's $R^4$ law $Q = \frac{\pi \Delta P R^4}{8\eta L}$ — doubling radius multiplies flow by $2^4 = 16$. A sphere settling in viscous fluid reaches Stokes terminal velocity $v_t = \frac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta} \propto r^2$. Micro-check: $2\ \text{Pa\,s} = 20\ \text{poise}$, and doubling a tube radius takes $Q$ up by $16\times$.

keyDefinitions.definition: Pressure measured relative to atmosphere: $\rho g h$ for a static liquid column.
Flow where each particle's path repeats: velocity at a point is time-independent; Bernoulli applies per streamline.
Incompressible and non-viscous — the regime where Bernoulli's theorem is exact.
Net upward force on an immersed body equal to the weight of displaced fluid.
Equilibrium of a floating body: total weight equals total upthrust.
Volume crossing a section per second, $Av$, constant along a steady incompressible pipe.
Shear stress per velocity gradient $\frac{F}{A\,dv/dy}$; SI unit Pa s, CGS unit poise.
Ordered layered flow vs chaotic eddies, judged by Reynolds number $\operatorname{Re} = \frac{\rho v D}{\eta}$ (low = laminar).
Constant settling speed when viscous drag plus upthrust balance weight; $v_t \propto r^2$ for a sphere.
Speed of liquid escaping a side orifice, $\sqrt{2gh}$ below the free surface (Torricelli).

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: The gauge pressure $10\ \text{m}$ below the surface of water ($\rho = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$) is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $\rho g h = 1000 \times 10 \times 10 = 10^5\ \text{Pa} = 100\ \text{kPa}$. Option C is the ATMOSPHERIC pressure — the absolute value would be about twice $10^5\ \text{Pa}$.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: A block of ice floating in a glass of pure water melts completely. The water level:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Floating ice already displaces water equal to its own weight, and melting converts it into exactly that volume of water — level unchanged. Rising needs trapped impurities or a lighter host liquid.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: Water flows at $3\ \text{m/s}$ through a pipe of radius $2\ \text{cm}$. In a section of radius $1\ \text{cm}$ the speed is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $A \propto r^2$: radius halved gives area $\tfrac{1}{4}$, so $v$ jumps $\times 4$ to $12\ \text{m/s}$ by $A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: A tank has an orifice $5\ \text{m}$ below the free surface ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$). The efflux speed is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Torricelli: $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 5} = 10\ \text{m/s}$ — free-fall speed from that depth.
$1\ \text{Pa\,s} = 10\ \text{poise}$, so $2\ \text{Pa\,s} = 20\ \text{poise}$. Reversing the factor picks the $0.2$ trap.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: In Poiseuille flow, doubling the tube radius multiplies the volume flow rate by:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $Q \propto R^4$: $2^4 = 16$. The $R^4$ leverage is the most-tested fluid fact.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: A sphere falling through a viscous liquid reaches terminal velocity $v_t$. Doubling its radius (same densities, same liquid) makes $v_t$:
A hydraulic press has pistons of area $5\ \text{cm}^2$ and $50\ \text{cm}^2$. A $20\ \text{N}$ force on the small piston lifts, on the large piston, a maximum load of:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $\frac{F_2}{F_1} = \frac{A_2}{A_1} = 10$, so $F_2 = 200\ \text{N}$. The large piston also moves only $\tfrac{1}{10}$ of the small piston's distance.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: Along a horizontal streamline of ideal flow, the speed doubles from $v$ to $2v$. The pressure change $P_2 - P_1$ equals:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $P_1 + \tfrac12\rho v^2 = P_2 + \tfrac12\rho(2v)^2 = P_2 + 2\rho v^2$, so $P_2 - P_1 = -\tfrac{3}{2}\rho v^2$: pressure drops by the difference of the speed heads.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: On heating, the viscosity of a LIQUID and of a GAS respectively:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Liquids lose cohesive strength (viscosity falls); gases gain molecular mixing (viscosity rises). The reversal is a classic conceptual option.

memoryHooks: Pressure at depth asks only HOW DEEP, never HOW WIDE — shape is irrelevant.
Pascal: squeeze a liquid and every wall feels the same squeeze.
Floating ice melting never raises pure-water level — its displacement is already its melt.
Narrow pipe = fast water: halve the radius, quarter the area, quadruple the speed.
Bernoulli is a ledger: pay speed or height, save pressure.
$1\ \text{Pa\,s} = 10\ \text{poise}$ — SI is ten times the poise, not a tenth.
Stokes terminal speed grows with $r^2$ — big raindrops outfall drizzle.
Heat a liquid, it thins; heat a gas, it thickens.
commonMistakes: Reporting absolute pressure ($P_0 + \rho gh$) when the question asks gauge — read the wording.
Assuming hydrostatic pressure depends on container shape or total liquid volume.
Scaling speed linearly with radius in continuity — it scales with $1/r^2$.
Using $Q \propto R^2$ instead of $R^4$ in Poiseuille problems.
Letting ice-melt water rise the level of pure water — it does not.
Forgetting the density difference $(\rho - \sigma)$ in Stokes terminal velocity.
Applying Bernoulli across viscous or unsteady flow without justification.
Treating faster flow as higher pressure on a horizontal streamline — it is lower.
examChecklist: Decide gauge vs absolute before computing $\rho g h$.
Continuity first: fix speeds from area ratios, then bring Bernoulli.
Efflux and free-fall share $\sqrt{2gh}$ — reuse the shortcut.
Convert viscosity units explicitly; write the $10\times$ factor down.
Poiseuille scaling: exponent 4 on radius, 1 on length and $\eta^{-1}$.
Stokes: check $\rho > \sigma$ for sinking, $\rho < \sigma$ for rising bubbles.
Ice-in-water level questions: unchanged, unless trapped mass or lighter liquid.
Bernoulli numerics on horizontal lines: subtract speed heads $\tfrac12\rho\Delta(v^2)$.
Hydraulic press: force gain = area ratio, displacement loss = same ratio.
Re-verify one arithmetic step with units carried through.
